tls.title: TLS endpoint
tls.heading: A TLS endpoint lives here
tls.leadHttps: The certificate this service presents, the client truststore it verifies against, and what this deployment does with a client certificate. This page is on the main HTTPS port, so there is no plain listener in this process: fetch the server certificate below without verifying it the first time, then trust it.
tls.leadHttp: The certificate this service presents, the client truststore it verifies against, and what this deployment does with a client certificate. This page is on the plain HTTP port, which is the one that is reachable before anything is trusted.
tls.listenError: A listener did not bind: {error}. This page is HTTP and answers either way; the listener does not.
tls.serverCertificateNote: Self-signed, and regenerated on every start — so it is an anchor nobody can have baked in. Fetch it and put it in your own truststore rather than switching verification off, which is the habit this whole workflow exists to break.
tls.subject: Subject
tls.verifiedAgainst: What client certificates are verified against
tls.verifiedAgainstNote: Empty at startup, and it has to be: the certificate authority whose clients this verifies is generated in a browser, minutes before the connection, and exists nowhere else. Paste its certificate here — the root, or the whole chain above the leaf.
tls.emptyStore: Empty. No client certificate can verify here yet, and nothing can connect to the listener that requires one.
tls.testControls: The two buttons are test controls, and a product process does not have them. The gated doors answer in every mode: POST /admin-api/tls/trust/add / remove, and the truststore page in the admin console, which also says where each anchor came from:
tls.worth: What a verified certificate is worth here
tls.worthNote: A verified client certificate means one thing: a chain was built from what the client sent to an anchor somebody supplied. No token is issued for presenting one, and this port requires nobody to present one at all. What it is good for is GET /tls/sign-in, which starts a sign-on session for its holder, and the doors that read a certificate for themselves: RFC 8705 client authentication at the token endpoint, /xacml and /scim/v2.
tls.recorded: It is also recorded, which is a different claim. When the handshake completes with a certificate that verified, the subject DN is filed as an authentication on /admin/users and the embedded LDAP directory seeds an entry for it — a certificate subject is already a DN, so it is the one identity here that does not have to be turned into one, and the subject, issuer, serial and validity go on the entry beside it. The directory service says where. Both are a record of what happened; neither is a credential.
forwarded.title: Forwarded headers
forwarded.heading: What a proxy told this service
forwarded.lead: The request as it arrived, and what was believed of it. Every issuer and every endpoint in both discovery documents is built from the effective base URL below, so if that is wrong, everything a client reads is wrong with it.
forwarded.proxyMust: What the proxy has to do
forwarded.document: the document built from that base URL
outcome.title: Truststore
outcome.added: {added, plural, one {# anchor added} other {# anchors added}}
outcome.addedNote: This service now verifies client certificates against {anchors, plural, one {# anchor} other {# anchors}}. Existing connections keep the truststore they were made under; the next handshake is judged against this one.
outcome.clearedNote: {removed, plural, one {# anchor removed} other {# anchors removed}}. No client certificate verifies here now: one presented to the main port still arrives, and everything that reads one refuses it — which is the state this service starts in.
